segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Elena died young. She was just 22. After her death, Von Cosel visited her grave every day and brought flowers. He built her a fancy mausoleum with a dome, surrounded by palm trees and flower pots.

segments.text: I talked to a guy named Ben Harrison. He wrote a book about the two of them. He lives in Key West and got curious about the case when he moved there. He says that von Cosel fell in love with Elena right away.

segments.text: A young man's lover died before their wedding. Without her love, he simply could not reason. At night, he would visit the graveyard and dream about the days she was alive.

segments.speaker: Ben Harrison
segments.text: His tears would fall upon her tombstone, the tombstone of the girl to be his bride. On a night when thunder roared and lightning flashed, he broke apart the tombstone of her grave. And with his hands, he dug into the earth, and in his arms, he carried her away. By a flickering funeral candlelight, on his bed that flowers covered, he gently laid the body of his sweetheart, and said his wedding vows to his dead lover.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The song was written to be tongue in cheek, ironic and inappropriate, but von Cosel took it literally, as inspiration for everything he's about to do next.

segments.speaker: Ben Harrison
segments.text: According to von Cosel, this is her plea for him to please take her home with him, the same way the distraught lover does in the song.

segments.speaker: Ben Harrison
segments.text: [SINGING IN SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Von Cosel wrote that he waited for a new moon, got a wagon, and stole the casket. He brought Elena home, and tried to repair her decomposed body.

segments.speaker: Ben Harrison
segments.text: Her face was in such poor shape that he had to do something, and so he put on this gauze wax concoction, and fastened it to what was left of her face.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He did this to the rest of her body too, inserted glass eyes and painted on eyebrows. Von Cosel hadn't been deterred by what Elena wanted back when she was alive. Now that he had her dead body in his home, he could play house, dress her up, have sex with her. And he did all of those things.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He wrote in his memoir that he made Elena breakfast, eggs and a cup of Lipton tea. He filled the vases next to her bed with flowers and sometimes just talked to her about the weather.

segments.speaker: Ben Harrison
segments.text: She was kind of his living doll, there in their little household. And they celebrated Christmas together, and he put a Christmas tree there, and put 13 candles and said he played his organ to her until the candles burned down.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: This went on for seven years. He also conducted experiments to try to bring Elena back from the dead. In his memoir, he wrote that he gave her radiation treatments, and submerged her in a tank filled with quote, plasma fluid.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Eventually, Elena's sister, Nana Medina, started to suspect that something was up. There were rumors. And she asked von Cosel to open Elena's mausoleum for her, but he refused. So one day, Nana showed up at his house.

segments.speaker: Ben Harrison
segments.text: Well, she walks in and sees this effigy, this Elena, in a sort of wedding, gauze wedding thing lying on the bed. I mean, as she describes it, it was the most horrific thing she'd ever seen in her life. But as upset as she was, she said, if you will take the body back and put it in there, we'll just let this go.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Von Cosel didn't return the body, so she went to the Key West police. They arrived at his house in a motorcade, and von Cosel confessed immediately.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And that's when the gifts started arriving at the jailhouse. People brought him fruit, cookies, and hot tea. They serenaded him at night. A group of women from Tampa brought him money. Locals posted his bond. An attorney took on his case pro bono.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: People were captivated by this story. A newspaper quoted von Cosel saying, "I did not want one so beautiful to go to dust." A radio station in Havana ran a soap opera about Elena and von Cosel's great romance.

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: He was in love with her? OK, he was in love with her and he wanted to make her better.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: This is Ida Roberts. Her mom was good friends with Elena, lived down the street from her. I talked to her for a while about this question. How could people see this as a romantic story?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Well, for starters, Ida's mom didn't know at the time that von Cosel was having sex with Elena's corpse. There were rumors, but the truth didn't come out for decades, when a doctor from her autopsy wrote about it in a medical journal. But still, that doesn't change the story so much for Ida.

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: My mother knew Maria Elena. And because she accepted him, my mother had no problem was with what he did.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I mean, was your mom upset that he had had the body for so long?

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: She was not upset.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: But isn't there something also later? The autopsy report came out he was having sexual relations with her, or attempting to?

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: Well, I guess he was in love with her, and he made love to her. And he didn't care whether she was dead or not. In fact, he never-- he never wanted to think that she was dead. He wanted to think that she was coming back. She was asleep.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I think, Ida, you are a very hard person to shock.

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: Yeah, mhm. Just remember, this was a very small town and very close. Everybody was very close. And I believe that's the way, laid back in Key West like we are, we just accept things.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I heard this from a lot of people I interviewed down there-- live and let live. They take pride in their history of being home to people who didn't fit in-- bootleggers, drug smugglers, people who dropped off the grid.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: But Ida's pretty straight. We talked in her office at a Catholic school in Key West. She's the director of Religious Education for kids there and looks like somebody's nice grandma.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: When you look at this story now, the story of von Cosel, I mean, do you view it as romantic or completely nuts?

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: I think it's a nice love story. I do. I wouldn't have any bad thing to say about him. [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Why is that? Explain that.

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: Because he was in love with her. I mean, he was eccentric of course, you know crazy thoughts he had, but I mean, he wasn't there to abuse her or anything. You know, I mean--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: According the record, he was.

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: Wait, but he didn't chop her up and throw her in the ocean or anything, like a lot of people have done, you know? A lot of spouses. But he took good care of her. And he wanted-- he just didn't want to let go.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I mean, definitely selfish, though. In a lot of ways, I mean, he's doing what he wants to do, and not necessarily what the family would have wanted her to do-- wanted him to do, or even Elena.

segments.speaker: Ida Roberts
segments.text: Love is like that. Love is kind of selfish, isn't it? When you find somebody you want, you want them regardless.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Love is an excuse for all sorts of behavior. I can understand why so many people wanted to believe this version of the story. It's much easier and nicer to see this as a grand gesture of a lovesick man than the abuse of a delusional pervert.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: In the end, the charges against von Cosel were dropped. The court looked into whether he was insane and decided no. They called his obsession with Elena a quirk.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Even when the public was presented with physical proof, Elena's body, they chose to see the story this way. After police took Elena's body from von Cosel, the funeral home, incredibly, put her out on display, probably without the family's permission.

segments.speaker: Don Carbonell
segments.text: It was a big crowd that day, I think, and we just followed the crowd.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: That's Don Carbonell. He was a kid at the time and lived across the street from the funeral home. There's actually a photo of Don in the newspaper spread, standing in a big crowd right behind Elena's body.

segments.speaker: Don Carbonell
segments.text: I might have even been playing in the yard with Frank, whose father owned the funeral home at the time. And they opened the embalming room doors.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And how close did you get?

segments.speaker: Don Carbonell
segments.text: I was probably six to ten feet away from the table that they had her laid up on.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And what do you remember? Do you remember what she looked like?

segments.speaker: Don Carbonell
segments.text: Yeah, vaguely, I remember. She had glassy eyes, and she just-- she didn't look real. She didn't look real. Looked like maybe somebody made up a body. That's the way she had impressed me. You'd say a big, overgrown doll.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The newspaper articles quoted people who said she looked beautiful. "Von Cosel did such a good job preserving her." One woman wrote a letter saying, "they should enclose Elena in a glass case and turn her into a Sleeping Beauty attraction." Which is basically what's happened to Elena and her story today.

segments.speaker: Key West Tour Guide
segments.text: All right, our story takes place here in 1930, and involves this young girl right here.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: This is from a trolley tour of Key West for tourists these days. All the disturbing facts of the story are now out. And our ideas about sex and men and women are dramatically different. But listen to this. They still tell this story as a romance, for the same reason people did in the '40s. They like it.

segments.speaker: Key West Tour Guide
segments.text: Well, I thought we'd discuss a love story, an undying love story, a story that involves grave robbing and a corpse bride. Who's interested? All right, good.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And here's another.

segments.speaker: Key West Tour Guide
segments.text: By show of hands, how many of you believe in true love? Just trying to set up this next tale-- this is a tale of true love, Key Weird style with a twist. It starts with a gentleman by the name of Count Karl von Cosel. Enter into the picture a beautiful Cuban girl. Her name is Elena.

segments.speaker: Key West Tour Guide
segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Miki Meek, Payson High School class of none of your business, is one of the producers of our program. John Ellison Conlee read the excerpts of von Cosel's memoir. Ben Harrison's book about von Cosel is called Undying Love.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, what happens when sky writers make mistakes, and a few grand gestures that actually go right. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program we choose a theme, bringing you a variety of different stories on that theme. Today's show, as we watch Valentine's Day recede into the rearview mirror of our lives, our theme is grand gestures, stories of people who go all out, and what it means when they do. We've arrived at Act Two of our program. Act 2, Say It Out Cloud.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of our producers, David Kestenbaum, spoke with some people who are in the grand gesture business. I'm talking about sky writers.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Every sky writer I talked to you had a story of some odd message they'd put in the sky. Someone paid for a cartoon cloud to be drawn in the sky, with little lines for rain. And then there was the message that was just numbers, 3.1415 etc. Get it? Pi in the sky.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The comedian Kurt Braunohler recently hired a pilot to put up the skywriting message over Los Angeles that he'd always wanted to see. "How do I land?"

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Even a simple message can cost a couple of thousand dollars. And it doesn't last very long. Basically, as soon as it's written, it starts to fall apart. So a lot of the time, it's people with a pretty big emotion who want to write something in the sky.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: It was the woman that contacted me, and she couldn't-- it was a very secret love affair.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This is Suzanne Asbury-Oliver. She's a longtime sky writer.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: And it couldn't be known that this relationship was happening.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: But she really wanted to express her commitment, almost in a public way that she couldn't in any other way. You know, shout out to the world "I love you and I'm with you forever." But nobody else can know.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The message? A heart. No name, just initials, in the sky over a lake.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: It was just kind of sad and romantic all at the same time.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Were they having an affair?

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: Well, that was my guess.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah. How did it feel doing that one?

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: Yeah, it was nice, you know? Letting somebody express a huge emotion.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In clouds of smoke.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: Yeah, mile-high letters, 10,000 feet above the Earth.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Sky writing seems to satisfy some very basic urge. Essentially, as soon as we figured out how to fly, someone was like, "You know what? I'm gonna write giant letters in the sky." The first pilot did it in the 1920s, maybe even earlier. And the vast majority of personal messages seem to be essentially the same thing over and over.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "Marry me," or "I love you," or a heart, or "I heart you." Here in New York, the usual spot is over Central Park. And it seems to be mostly guys who want to put messages of love in the sky. The male sky writers I talked to didn't have a lot of theories about why that was. But Suzanne did.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: Maybe men have a harder time expressing themselves? And want to say "I really, really, really do love you. I really, really do want you to marry me" in a really big way.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: This is it. These are our airplanes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Only a handful of people in the world do sky writing. It's this weirdly technical piece of flying. I went to visit Jim Record he's a pilot with a company called Skytypers out on Long Island. It was snowing out, so we weren't going up. But he showed me one of the planes.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: OK, this is our lead airplane.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: How do you get in? Climb up on the wing?

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE] yeah.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The plane looks like he stole it from a museum. It's a World War II plane, built in 1940. Imagine someone wearing goggles and a long scarf flying it, trying to shoot down another pilot. There's a spot on the wings where the machine guns would have been mounted. He let me climb in.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This just got super real.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: Oh, it's real. Yeah, this got super real in a hurry.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And where's the button for the smoke?

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: Right here.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Can I press it?

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: Sure

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: [CLICKING]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There's a very small fire extinguisher here.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: That fire extinguisher, if you can't put it out with that thing, then you jump out of the airplane.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Jim's a former Navy pilot. He once applied to be an astronaut. Every skywriting job, he and the other pilots, they call it a mission.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: From his perspective, the key to a successful marriage proposal is pre-mission planning. Because in order for the message to look right from the ground, he has to write it backward. That's how it looks to him up there. He's looking down, and everyone else is looking up. The order of the letters is backward for him, and the letters themselves are backward.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Jim says he tries not to think about that. It's just too confusing. So he'll break it down into a series of moves that he can just execute.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: M's are tough, because there's so much involved in an M. There's actually four different strokes in an M. And then the R's aren't all that easy either, because you do an R, and then you have to come around and go here, and you've got to come up and it comes down here again.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "Marry me." Two M's, two R's. Jim will climb into this tiny plane with me "Marry me" or whatever mapped out on a piece of paper on a clipboard. When he's in the right spot, he makes sure the Arm Smoke switch has been flipped. Then he presses that little button under his thumb on the stick, and streaming out behind him is this giant tube of perfectly white, billowy smoke.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: To make sure the letters are the right length, he counts.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: Smoke on, thousand one, thousand two, thousand three, thousand four. I start tightening the turn ups. Five, six--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He's describing how he draws a heart here, one side at a the time. He'll start at the top, where the two halves are going to come together, turning, turning, almost in a circle, then straightening out.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: 15, 16, smoke off.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Since his plane is, in effect, the tip of the pencil, Jim can't actually see how what he's writing looks. So when he's done half the heart, he'll pull back on the stick, and shoot up higher into the sky, to the point where the airplane almost stalls. He says at this point, he's upside down, looking down at the message, which, remember, is backward. Then he'll basically dive bomb back down and do the other half of the heart.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Are there are a lot of tight turns? Would I get sick?

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: It's all tight turns. Yes, you would get sick. It's not normal. You spend a lot of time upside down and backwards.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Do you ever screw up?

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: Oh, yes. Unfortunately, I have.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One time-- he knows this is silly. One time, he made a mistake, and then went back to cross it out-- like flew across the whole message and laid down another line of smoke through what he'd written.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Greg Stinis, another sky writer, told me he once mixed up two marriage proposals. He can't remember the names, but it was like, he wrote "Marry me, Sue," and the woman below was named Tabitha, and vice versa.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Another time, he did this happy face over the Macy's Day parade in New York City. It looked great, but then the wind started to twist the face until it looked like a creepy demon. He flew back and forth through it, to try to get it to disperse, but it hung around for a long time.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: There are darker emotions people sometimes want to put in the sky. One pilot told me about a woman who thought her boyfriend was cheating on her. She wanted to write "I'm watching you" above his head. And Suzanne Asbury-Oliver, whose company, by the way, is Oliver's Flying Circus, told me about this request she got just last month.

segments.speaker: Suzanne Asbury-oliver
segments.text: Yeah, I got a request, actually they wanted it over the inaugural. And it was "[BLEEP Trump."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: She said no. And for all the marriage proposals sky writers get, Jim says there is also this one.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: We've done one divorce. And the divorce message was, "She got it all."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That seem sad to you?

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: No no. I can't say it did, since I've been divorced before. Everybody says the happiest times of a boat owner-- the day they buy it, and the day they sell it. I would think maybe a marriage would be like that-- the day you get married and the day you finally are not married.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Can you imagine the guy looking up and being like, I did it.

segments.speaker: Jim Record
segments.text: It's a defiant stand. It's like, yes, but the last $5,000 you didn't get, because I put it into this message.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One emotion did seem kind of absent in all the stories I heard, for reasons that I totally get, because it's hard enough to do this in letters that aren't a mile high, which is to say "I'm sorry."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Jim's boss, Larry Arken, did remember one like that. It was from years ago, but it stuck with him. The message "Pooh Bear, come home." They wrote it in two or three spots around New York.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He thinks some guy's girlfriend or wife had left him. He doesn't know how it turned out. But I have a guess. I think when you are to the point of writing something like that, with giant letters in the sky, you are probably past the point where giant letters in the sky can help you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum. [MUSIC PLAYING - "SKY WRITING"]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 3, It's Gesture Imagination. More than anybody on our staff, maybe more than anybody I've ever met, actually, one of our producers, Elna Baker, really, truly believed in the power of grand gestures. It was this kind of magical thinking that lasted well into adulthood for her, into her late 20s.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I believed that it was the surest way to show someone you love them or to win love.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And a grand gesture could be, like, what?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: A declaration of love, like a speech, but in a very public manner. A giant cardboard sign. Showing someone that you especially knew them through a very special gift.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Elna grew up Mormon. And talking to her about how she loves grand gestures made me think of those kids from Payson High School. Remember them? We started today's program with them. Lots of those kids are Mormon. And the way they ask each other to dances at that school happens all over Utah. And it occurred to me, is there something about being young and Mormon and grand gestures that go together?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And this isn't something you could prove one way or another, but just to say it, you have these kids who are forbidden to drink or have sex. Maybe that's one reason that their feelings for each other play out with these elaborate schemes, right? And that made sense to Elna.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah. No, I definitely-- once I started having sex, I stopped doing grand gestures. Because I was like, oh, turns out you can just-- [MUMBLING] You know? You could just have sex with someone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That made it weird dirtier, the way you just said that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I grew up on grand-- like my parents, the way my parents got together was-- I grew up on stories of grand gestures.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, is that true?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like what?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: My dad and mom dated for about two and a half weeks. And my dad went to the Mormon temple, and he was just praying to see if he should date this woman. And he said that he heard the voices of his future children, like me and my brothers and sisters, and we were like, hurry, go, do it. Like, we want to be born.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah. And he rushed out of the temple, went and found my mom, knocked on her door, brought her outside of her dorm. And in front of the dorm, there was a rock, like a big rock. And he made her stand on top of the rock. And then he knelt down and said, "Will you marry me?" And she said yes.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: They'd been dating for two and a half weeks. They've known each other for four weeks. And my parents actually are very in love, and very happily married. And so I believed that love was like hearing a voice that basically told you this was right. And then you would do anything for that voice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And that's the attitude towards love Elna carried into adulthood. When she would talk to our friends about their romantic lives and situations, at some point, Elna would tell them, OK, here's what you have to do. You have to go big. And she'd give advice that, today, she thinks was totally wrong headed. Up until her 20s, she had no experience in love, had never had a real adult relationship, was completely naive about all of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But she still cheerfully jumped in with her advice. She encouraged her friend Nick to move to New York City to prove his love for a woman who had broken up with him and did not want his love. She convinced your friend Allie to give a guy that she'd just started seeing this giant birthday crown, homemade with fur and feathers and a star with his picture that kind of jumped off the crown. He never went out with Allie again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When Elna's friend Louise regretted breaking up with her boyfriend, Gabe, and decided she wanted Gabe back, Elna suggested a gift. She remembered that a couple months before they had found this vintage 1970s-era McDonald's uniform in his exact size. And he'd had all these stories of working at McDonald's in high school. So Louise bought this thing for him, to give as a present on Halloween, but never gave it to him.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: So he got it from the closet, and I was like, what you have to do is go over to his apartment and leave it at his door. He'll get it. He'll know that you get him, and you love him.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, when you suggested this to her, what was her attitude about it?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: That's a terrible idea. She was very, very resistant. But then this thing happens when you're with me, apparently, where I just got her all spun up into the idea.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Your air of confidence drew her in.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Totally. It's like I put her in a box and shook the box, and then-- or when a kid is going to play pinata, and you turn them around and then push them in the direction--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of the pinata. That's what you did to her.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: That's what I did to her, where she eventually just started getting excited about the gesture itself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which is key. It became about the bold thing that they were doing, versus how Gabe would feel. And it worked out about as well as you would expect. Louise left the box with the gift for Gabe, with no note-- just left it in his building.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so they met up and had this huge blow out fight, where she was like, how come you didn't thank me for the gift? And he was just like, you totally broke my heart. You crushed me. And it actually is offensive that you think that this gift could just instantly make up for all of that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Were you surprised?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Shocked. I was waiting like a puppy at the door for her to come in and tell me, thank me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And she walked in, and she was crying, and totally devastated, heartbroken.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Elna didn't just organize these kinds of schemes for other people. She did them herself. Like, one time, she was taking tickets as a page for The Letterman Show and met this random guy.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: He was in line to see the show, and we talked very briefly. And I thought I heard a voice that said, "This is who you are meant to be with."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She knew, of course, from her parents to trust that voice. So she gave this guy her number and dated him for a month and a half, and it went nowhere. Then, two years later, still hung up on this guy, who'd moved to Zambia, she wrote him an email.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Which I have here. Do you want me to read the email I wrote?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Totally.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: All right. "I don't know if you're still in Zambia, but my girlfriends and I are going to South Africa in the spring to visit some family friends of mine. I'm not sure how far Zambia is from South Africa, but if it's close, I'd love to come up and say hi. It'd be fun to see you. It's been a while. I hope you're well. X, Elna."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But OK, I did not have a trip to Africa planned.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you have some sort of friends in South Africa?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: No, made that up entirely.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then "I don't know if Zambia is near South Africa." Did you actually look on a map?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, OK.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But that's why I chose South Africa.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She roped two girlfriends into this trip, spent all her money, thousands of dollars on plane tickets. They stayed at this guy's little studio apartment, and on the very first night of a 10 day visit, she snuck over to his sleeping bag, woke him up, and tried to kiss him.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And he said, I think this is a bad idea.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so what were the next nine days like?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Really uncomfortable. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then there was the time that Elna tried to drag her friend Heather into pursuing a guy with one of these capers. Heather was one of the friends that Elna took on that trip to Africa. She was a page at The Letterman Show. And Elna would sometimes ask her--

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Who do you like? Or tell me about your relationships. And she was always really vague about it. And she would just say that she'd been in love before, but it just hadn't worked out.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so I kept fishing for details. Eventually, after a few months, I got out that they were college sweethearts. They'd been together about five years. And it just hadn't worked out.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so I kept trying to strategize. I was like, OK, well, we gotta-- if you still love him, we're going to make this work out. What can we do to show him how you feel?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What did you suggest that she might do?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, I asked well, when are you planning a trip home? Can you see him? No, I can't see him. Well, why not?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then after, maybe six, seven months of this, one day she said, "Look, I feel really bad for not having told you this, but the reason it didn't work out is that he died in a forest fire." And yeah, and they were planning on getting married. He was her whole life, her whole future. She imagined having kids with him.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Although I will say in retrospect, I was like a goldfish. I blinked my eyes, and I was like, well? Like, I took the information, and I was like, well, have you liked anyone since?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Very sensitive.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, I asked her if, in the time since-- which I think had been about two years.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the answer was yes, one guy. It was before she moved to New York. She was working at a little puddle jumper airport in Idaho, and was checking in this guy for a flight. And they started talking, had this really nice talk for 45 minutes.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: When he was on the airplane, she looked up the roster, found his name, and found that in a week, he was going be flying back through the same airport. So she changed her schedule, made sure she was working at that time, got all dressed up, waited a whole day. He didn't fly through. That was it.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so she finishes the story, and I was like, this is the worst story I've ever heard. That was it?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is the most tragic. Right, because it seemed like true love to you?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because, just to review, you hadn't been in love yourself yet?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, but I'd been in love at a glance.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's as far as you had gone.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, and it feels-- ah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then Heather admitted she'd googled the guy, found that he worked at a river guiding company. He was in a picture on their website. And every now and then, she would look at the picture. And Elna, of course, was like, great. You know his name. You know where he works. Time to act. Heather responded in the way I think most rational people would.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She was like, this dude does not remember me. Like, I'm sure this dude doesn't remember me. It had been like a year and a half since they'd spoken once for 45 minutes. And I was like, well, you never know unless you try. And so I kept at her for, I think, like four months or so, I just kept being like, just write the letter, write the letter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then one day, Heather was visiting Elna's apartment, and Elna pulled out a box of fancy stationery.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And I was like, OK, I know we're not going to send this letter, but if we did send it, what would we say? And so I gave her--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So sly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And did she see through your clever stratagem?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, she played along.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then Heather was like, how do you get over the problem that I'm writing a letter to this guy a year and a half after we met each other totally out of the blue? Well, here's the letter Elna wrote.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: "Hey, um, you probably don't remember me. We met at the airport. And I made a misstep, missed the opportunity to connect with you then, and it just so happened a year and a half later my younger brother is thinking of being a river guide. And we were looking on sites of river guides, and I came across this picture. And I was like, wait, how do I know that guy?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, I saw him at an airport a year and a half ago. And I thought, wow. I missed that chance then. Let me write him a letter now. So I just wanted to say hello, and you know, here's my email if you ever want to connect."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: The part that was a lie was her brother wasn't interested in being a river guide.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also, of course, the whole rest of it, stumbling across this picture accidentally, the whole thing. Over the next few months, they drafted and redrafted this letter. And it was like a game. They would show it to people. They would get edits and suggestions.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then one day, Heather calls Elna and tells her she sent the letter. And really, for the first time, Elna realized, oh wait, maybe this is a bad idea.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I don't know. It hit me in that moment that sending the letter would mean that Heather was going to get hurt. And I felt really nervous.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. Because every other time you've tried this, it's failed.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And suddenly you realize, oh, she's going to be hurt, and she was feeling OK, and now I got her hopes up.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And she's going to feel bad, and it's my fault.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Exactly. Yeah, but then at the same time, I also felt proud of her. Because this was the first-- I felt like she put her heart out again. I guess the consolation in that moment was, this probably isn't going to work out, but she showed the universe, or whatever, that she's willing to try again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, she showed herself that she's willing to try again after all the sadness that she'd had with her boyfriend. So does she end up getting a boyfriend after that?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, so two weeks later the guy who got the letter wrote back.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And it was actually pretty short and friendly. He remembered meeting her, and she left an impression on him too. And they started dating. And they dated for seven years, and now they're married.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, that's the end of the story?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, they actually got together.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I know. I gave a toast at their wedding, where I told this story of writing the letter. It's kind of the most magical thing that I've ever helped facilitate.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, so that worked with her. Do you think these kinds of things are a good idea?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Grand gestures?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: No, not anymore. And actually, I think it worked--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, wait, I'm confused now. Why are they a bad idea?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It seems false. It's not really how you show someone you love them in the way I thought it was. I feel like it has more to do with you than the other person.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She actually hasn't done this stuff now in almost a decade, doesn't miss it. And when she looks back on it, she thinks she was doing those big gestures because she was so unsure of herself.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I was afraid that they wouldn't like me, if I just was like, hey, I'm interested in you. This is who I am. I thought maybe you like construction paper, and giant signs, and hot glue gun art.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And if I'd show you all of that and I'm standing behind it, then if I'm not enough, at least you'll like that, and you'll say yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's scary being real with another person. And there are so many ways to avoid it. This is just a particularly splashy one.
